WHY IT HAPPENS, mechanically. A gate discharge is a *local* edit — one new instance in one
new module — but the claim it falsifies is *distributed*: every consumer docstring, the
module docstring above it, the campaign plan, the axiom-probe section header, the root
roll-up's import comment, and the hgraph node synced from the docstring. Nothing links them,
so the closing session sees a green build and a correct new file.

WHY IT IS EXPENSIVE, and it is not symmetric with `I-0349`. Both directions mislead a
reader, but this one misleads the *planner*: "the frontier is four leaves" is the sentence a
later session quotes when budgeting, and it over-counts remaining work by a factor. Two
sessions were briefed against stale frontier counts before this was noticed. Over-counting
open work is the failure that wastes a lane; under-counting merely wastes a grep.

THE DISCIPLINE, for the session that closes a gate — cheap, and it is your job, not the
janitor's:

    grep -rn '<GateName>' <project> --include=*.lean --include=*.md --include=*.tex

Read every hit, not just the file you edited. Include `informal/`, `scripts/`, the root
roll-up module, and the blueprint. Any hit that describes the gate's STATUS (rather than
using it) is now suspect. A hit in a file outside your write set is an inbox ask to its
owner in the same session — do not leave it, and do not assume the owner will notice.

COROLLARY FOR MEMORY ITEMS THEMSELVES. `I-0381` recorded "the frontier is FOUR statements",
was corrected to ONE, then to zero — wrong twice in one day, in the same direction. Do not
put a frontier COUNT in a durable memory. Record the technique and the tooling; point at the
roadmap row for the count, which is the thing designed to be re-set.

WHY IT HAPPENS, mechanically. A gate discharge is a *local* edit — one new instance in one
new module — but the claim it falsifies is *distributed*: every consumer docstring, the
module docstring above it, the campaign plan, the axiom-probe section header, the root
roll-up's import comment, and the hgraph node synced from the docstring. Nothing links them,
so the closing session sees a green build and a correct new file.

WHY IT IS EXPENSIVE, and it is not symmetric with `I-0349`. Both directions mislead a
reader, but this one misleads the *planner*: "the frontier is four leaves" is the sentence a
later session quotes when budgeting, and it over-counts remaining work by a factor. Two
sessions were briefed against stale frontier counts before this was noticed. Over-counting
open work is the failure that wastes a lane; under-counting merely wastes a grep.

THE DISCIPLINE, for the session that closes a gate — cheap, and it is your job, not the
janitor's:

    grep -rn '<GateName>' <project> --include=*.lean --include=*.md --include=*.tex

Read every hit, not just the file you edited. Include `informal/`, `scripts/`, the root
roll-up module, and the blueprint. Any hit that describes the gate's STATUS (rather than
using it) is now suspect. A hit in a file outside your write set is an inbox ask to its
owner in the same session — do not leave it, and do not assume the owner will notice.

COROLLARY FOR MEMORY ITEMS THEMSELVES. `I-0381` recorded "the frontier is FOUR statements",
was corrected to ONE, then to zero — wrong twice in one day, in the same direction. Do not
put a frontier COUNT in a durable memory. Record the technique and the tooling; point at the

WHY IT HAPPENS, mechanically. A gate discharge is a *local* edit — one new instance in one
new module — but the claim it falsifies is *distributed*: every consumer docstring, the
module docstring above it, the campaign plan, the axiom-probe section header, the root
roll-up's import comment, and the hgraph node synced from the docstring. Nothing links them,
so the closing session sees a green build and a correct new file.

WHY IT IS EXPENSIVE, and it is not symmetric with `I-0349`. Both directions mislead a
reader, but this one misleads the *planner*: "the frontier is four leaves" is the sentence a
later session quotes when budgeting, and it over-counts remaining work by a factor. Two
sessions were briefed against stale frontier counts before this was noticed. Over-counting
open work is the failure that wastes a lane; under-counting merely wastes a grep.

THE DISCIPLINE, for the session that closes a gate — cheap, and it is your job, not the
janitor's:

    grep -rn '<GateName>' <project> --include=*.lean --include=*.md --include=*.tex

Read every hit, not just the file you edited. Include `informal/`, `scripts/`, the root
roll-up module, and the blueprint. Any hit that describes the gate's STATUS (rather than
using it) is now suspect. A hit in a file outside your write set is an inbox ask to its
owner in the same session — do not leave it, and do not assume the owner will notice.

COROLLARY FOR MEMORY ITEMS THEMSELVES. `I-0381` recorded "the frontier is FOUR statements",
was corrected to ONE, then to zero — wrong twice in one day, in the same direction. Do not
put a frontier COUNT in a durable memory. Record the technique and the tooling; point at the
roadmap row for the count, which is the thing designed to be re-set.
